paragraphs: The sage Narada once asked Krishna to show him Maya, the great illusion. A few days later Krishna invited Narada on a walk toward the desert. After several miles, Krishna said he was thirsty and asked Narada to bring him some water. Narada promised to go at once.

Close by was a village. Narada knocked at a door, and it was opened by a lovely young woman. The moment he saw her, he forgot all about his Master waiting thirsty in the desert. He stood there chatting with her and spent the whole day at the house. The conversation turned into love. He asked her father for her hand, they were married, and they settled down there and had children.

Twelve years went by. His father-in-law died and Narada inherited the property. He had his wife and children, his fields and cattle, and he seemed to himself to be living a very happy life. Then the flood came.

One night the river burst its banks and swept through the village. Houses collapsed, and people and animals were carried off and drowned. Narada fled, holding his wife with one hand and two children with the other, with a third child on his shoulders, and tried to wade across the raging water. A few steps in, the current proved too strong. The child on his shoulders slipped and was swept away. Trying to save him, Narada lost hold of another child. At last even his wife was torn from his arms, and he was thrown onto the bank, sobbing in despair.

Then, from behind him, came a gentle voice. It was Krishna, asking for His water. Narada had gone to fetch it, He said, and had been gone almost half an hour. Half an hour! In Narada's mind, twelve whole years had passed. That, Swamiji said, is Maya.
learn: We can get so absorbed in the drama of daily life, its gains and losses and plans, that we forget what we set out to do. Every now and then, step back and ask whether you are still on your original errand.
